clue.text: Fish with worm's tail for a spell

parts.note: the char is a fish of the trout family

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, here taken from worm's

explanation.surface: An angler pairs a fish with the tail end of a worm for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a spell' reads as 'for a while', but 'spell' is the definition, in the sense of an enchantment.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm is a magical incantation, the same thing as a spell cast by a witch.

clue.text: Play the part of a custodian

explanation.surface: An actor takes on the role of a caretaker of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter wrote a famous play of this name; the word also means a person looking after a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter's 1960 drama bears this title; a janitor or warden looks after premises as custodian.

clue.text: The price once of some spirit?

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a measure of liquor used to cost.
explanation.walkthrough: The angel was an old English gold coin; 'spirit' suggests drink but means a heavenly being.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English gold coin once paid as a price; a heavenly messenger is a spirit.

clue.text: Walker's not in this procession

parts.note: a pedestrian has no place in a parade made up entirely of motor vehicles

explanation.surface: A marcher is excluded from a parade.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorcade is a procession of cars, so nobody on foot takes part.

clue.text: Perhaps some fire in an inferior novel?

explanation.surface: A reader finds a few flames inside a poorly written book.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, a fire under a cooking pot heats it; the hyphenated word is also slang for hack fiction written just to earn money.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire is one example of a heat source for a cooking vessel; hack fiction churned out for income is called by the same hyphenated name.

clue.text: View of features for the papers

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a file is a folder of papers

explanation.surface: A side view of someone's face is offered to the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the papers' suggests newspapers, but it is a file of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A profile is a side-on outline of a person's face, a view of their features.

clue.text: Bear witness to rise of youth leader? Well put

indicators.note: in a down clue, a rise means the pieces are read upwards, so backwards
a leader is the first letter, here of youth

parts.note: well, as in healthy, means fit
to put something down is to set it

explanation.surface: Someone testifies to the promotion of a youth group's head, and phrases it nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise of' turns the whole run Y + FIT + SET upwards, giving TESTIFY.
explanation.definitionFit: To testify is to give evidence on oath, as a witness does in court.

clue.text: Ape, in short, has no end of fruit

indicators.note: has no end of means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: an orange is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A monkey, put briefly, has endless fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' marks the definition as an abbreviation: the orang-utan.
explanation.definitionFit: Orang is a shortened form of orang-utan, the great ape of Borneo and Sumatra.

clue.text: Book-keeper who records loans, perhaps

parts.note: reads as an accountant logging lending, but it is someone who keeps books and notes which have been borrowed

explanation.surface: An accountant tracks money lent out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book-keeper' suggests an accountant; read literally, it is someone who looks after books.
explanation.definitionFit: A person in charge of a lending collection of books keeps them and logs each borrowing.

clue.text: Old characters nurse maltreated

indicators.note: maltreated means badly handled, so the letters of nurse are knocked about

explanation.surface: Elderly people were treated badly by a nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old characters' suggests elderly people; it means ancient written letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are letters of an ancient Germanic alphabet, old written characters.

clue.text: Like this rogue reformed

indicators.note: reformed means formed again, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scoundrel who has mended their ways is now virtuous.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a rogue who has reformed is morally upright, and 'reformed' rearranges THIS ROGUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A reformed villain has become virtuous and morally upright.

clue.text: Vestment taken by an old-time saint

indicators.note: the vestment is taken by, so followed by, the word an

parts.note: an alb is a white linen vestment worn by priests

explanation.surface: A priestly garment is borrowed by a saint from long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: St Alban is venerated as the first British Christian martyr.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban was a Roman-era martyr, Britain's earliest recorded saint.

clue.text: Peasant leader in merely temporary retirement

indicators.note: retirement means withdrawing backwards, so the hidden run is read in reverse
in signals letters sitting inside the words merely temporary

explanation.surface: A rebel chief has gone into hiding, but only for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: Wat Tyler led the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
explanation.definitionFit: Wat Tyler was the leader of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt in England.

clue.text: Gelatine is where you'd expect to find beer

parts.words: where you'd expect to find beer
parts.note: beer is served in a glass, giving the phrase 'in glass'

explanation.surface: A brewer explains that gelatine is found where beer would be.
explanation.walkthrough: Isinglass, a gelatine made from fish bladders, is genuinely used to clear beer, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Isinglass is a pure form of gelatine obtained from fish air bladders, used for fining.

clue.text: Getting money for relatives in Irish port?

parts.note: kin are one's relatives
a sale is how one gets money for goods

explanation.surface: Someone raises cash for their family in an Irish harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Kinsale is a harbour town in County Cork, Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Kinsale is a historic harbour town on the south coast of County Cork.

clue.text: Stationery requirement of the Bank of England

definitions.text: requirement of the Bank of England

explanation.surface: The Bank of England needs office supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: Writing sheets are stationery; the Bank of England needs paper to print banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing sheets are stationery; the Bank of England prints banknotes on special paper.

clue.text: Opening speaker looking bored?

explanation.surface: The first speaker at an event looks weary.
explanation.walkthrough: A wide gap is described with the same word as a person opening their mouth from boredom.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaping chasm is wide open; a tired orator stretching the mouth wide shows boredom.

clue.text: Old German title — glad Vera West translated it

indicators.note: translated means changed into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Vera from the West is pleased to render an old German title.
explanation.walkthrough: A waldgrave was a German count with jurisdiction over a royal forest.
explanation.definitionFit: A waldgrave was a medieval German noble rank, a count in charge of forests.

clue.text: Beat up the joiners of course!

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: to beat is to flog
links are things that join

explanation.surface: Someone attacks the carpenters, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course!' looks like an exclamation, but 'course' is the definition, a golf course; 'joiners' suggests carpenters.
explanation.definitionFit: Links is a term for a seaside golf course.

clue.text: Was beaten by inferior force, perhaps

definitions.text: Was beaten by inferior force, perhaps

parts.words: Was beaten by inferior force, perhaps
parts.note: a cryptic description of an army pulling back, here framed as defeat at the hands of a weaker opponent

explanation.surface: A superior army suffers defeat at the hands of a smaller one.
explanation.definitionFit: An army that withdraws in defeat falls back from its position.

clue.text: Dealings in jam?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether there is trading in preserves.
explanation.walkthrough: Traffic means trade, and it is also what sits stuck in a road jam.
explanation.definitionFit: Illegal trading is called trafficking; vehicles held up in a road jam are traffic.

clue.text: Soldier sounds nutty

indicators.note: sounds signals the word is said aloud, giving a soldier's rank that is pronounced the same

parts.note: a kernel is the edible inside of a nut, so nutty here points to that word

explanation.surface: A soldier's speech comes across as rather mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nutty' looks like an adjective meaning crazy, but it leads to the nut's kernel, which is pronounced like the officer rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonel is a senior army officer, a soldier ranking above a major.

clue.text: "And thinner, --, farther going!" (Tennyson)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Tennyson's Bugle Song in The Princess, describing horn notes growing fainter

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson's poetry with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Tennyson's 'The splendour falls', the Bugle Song: 'O hark, O hear! how thin and clear, / And thinner, clearer, farther going!'
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's line uses comparatives: the bugle's notes grow thinner, purer and more distant.

clue.text: Apt clue I'd maybe copy

indicators.note: maybe signals that the letters of these words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A setter wonders whether a fitting clue of theirs might be copied.
explanation.definitionFit: A replica or reproduction of something is an exact copy of the original.

clue.text: Garments disliked by cricketers

explanation.surface: Cricketers don't like certain clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Ducks are trousers made of a strong linen cloth; in cricket a duck is a score of nought, which batsmen hate.
explanation.definitionFit: Light canvas trousers are called ducks; a batsman's zero score is a duck, which no cricketer wants.

clue.text: Angry Hook losing his head

indicators.note: losing his head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: Captain Hook in Peter Pan is a pirate

explanation.surface: Captain Hook is furious and loses control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing his head' sounds like losing one's temper, apt for an angry man, but it drops the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate means furious, very angry.

clue.text: Note form of transport sought by knights of old

parts.note: G is a note of the musical scale
rail is a form of transport, travel by train

explanation.surface: Knights of the past looked for a written message about travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' suggests a written message, but it is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy Grail was the sacred cup that Arthurian knights quested after.

clue.text: Foreigner can spell aright

parts.note: split as 'a right': the word a, taken as it is
a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: An outsider is able to spell correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aright' means correctly, but split into two words it is 'a right', and a lien is a legal right over property.
explanation.definitionFit: An alien is a foreign national, a person from another country.

clue.text: Constable, the painter, has source of oil

parts.note: a constable is a policeman, slang cop
RA, Royal Academician, stands for a painter

explanation.surface: John Constable, the landscape artist, is said to own a source of oil paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable, the painter' suggests the English landscape artist John Constable; split, it is a police officer plus a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Copra is dried coconut kernel, pressed to extract coconut oil.

clue.text: Structure of aeroplanes in flight perhaps

explanation.surface: Someone describes how aircraft are arranged as they fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means a structure or arrangement in general, and also the pattern that aircraft fly in together.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrangement or build-up is a structure; planes flying in a set pattern fly in one.

clue.text: Desire transport?

parts.note: refers to the Tennessee Williams play about a tram named Desire, so the vehicle bearing that name

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether longing can carry them away.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennessee Williams's play is titled after a New Orleans tram on the Desire line.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tennessee Williams's play, the tram named Desire is a vehicle of public transport.

clue.text: Irish town's sporting set without a leader

definitions.note: the possessive reads as 'Irish town is'

indicators.note: without a leader means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a set is a unit of play in tennis, so a sporting set points to that game

explanation.surface: A town in Ireland has a sports team with no captain.
explanation.walkthrough: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis is a market town in the west of Ireland, the seat of County Clare.
